title: Leader-Based Replication
explain: In leader-based replication, one replica, the leader, accepts every write, and the other replicas, the followers, copy its replication log and apply it in the same order. Because exactly one node decides write order, replicas cannot disagree about it and there are no write-write conflicts between them. It scales reads and gives simple semantics, but writes still go through one node.
model:
My analogy: one editor and several proofreaders who only get copies. The editor's version is the truth, and copies lag by the delivery time.

```
clients ─writes─▶ LEADER ──replication log──▶ follower 1
                    │                     └─▶ follower 2
clients ─reads──▶ leader or followers (maybe stale)
```

- **Reads scale** by adding followers; **writes do not** (to scale writes, [shard](#/sd/f/sharding) as well).
- **Followers can be stale**, depending on sync or async replication.
- **Losing the leader** needs a failover, which risks lost writes and two leaders at once.
- **Log formats:** statement-based (breaks on `NOW()` and `RAND()`), physical WAL shipping (exact but version-coupled), logical row-based (portable, the usual choice).
- **Adding a follower never pauses the leader:** consistent snapshot tagged with a log position, copy it, replay everything after that position.

The four sub-topics: [write path](#/sd/f/leader-based-write-path), [read path](#/sd/f/leader-based-read-path), [consistency](#/sd/f/leader-based-consistency), [failover](#/sd/f/leader-based-failover). Contrast [multi-leader](#/sd/f/multi-leader-replication) and [leaderless](#/sd/f/leaderless-replication).

details.q: My primary is at 95% CPU from writes. Will adding followers help?
details.a: No. Every follower must still apply every write, so writes do not get cheaper; they get slightly more expensive. Followers only offload reads. Scale writes by sharding or by reducing write cost.

details.q: What is the throughput ceiling of a single leader?
details.a: Write capacity divided by the write fraction. A leader that commits 2,000 writes/s with a 4% write workload supports at most 2,000 / 0.04 = 50,000 total requests/s, if followers absorb all the reads.

details.q: Why does one leader remove write conflicts, and what does that cost?
details.a: One node sequences all writes, so every replica applies the same order and there is nothing to reconcile. The cost is a write bottleneck and a single point of write failure that needs failover.

Re-executing `UPDATE ... SET started_at = NOW()` on each follower yields different values on each. Non-deterministic functions, triggers and auto-increments diverge; row-based logical logs ship the result, not the statement.

details.q: How do you add a follower without pausing the leader?
details.a: Take a consistent snapshot that records its log position, copy it to the new node, then have the follower request all log entries after that position and replay until it catches up.

details.q: Sync vs async followers: what is the trade-off?
details.a: Sync waits for follower acks (durable, slower, a slow follower can stall writes); async acknowledges after local commit (fast, but an acknowledged write can be lost if the leader dies first). See the write path.

prompts.q: Explain leader-based replication and what you gain and lose compared with a single node.
points: One leader orders all writes, followers apply the log

prompts.q: Walk through adding a new follower to a live database.
points: Consistent snapshot with a log position
Copy snapshot to the new node
Replay log entries after that position
Join the read pool only when caught up

prompts.q: Your database is write-bound. Say what does and does not help.
points: Move reads off the leader to free capacity
